# Results — Study 352 (Opening-Range Breakout)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The viral 5-minute opening-range
breakout (ORB), tested on real intraday data and — crucially — against a **same-exposure random
entry** on the same days. Mark the high/low of the first R minutes; go long on a break above /
short below; hold to the close (one execution lag). Offline & deterministic given the cache;
run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance 5-minute bars (Yahoo public endpoint, no key) — **QQQ** (headline), SPY (cross-check) |
| As-of | 2026-06-22 (bars through 2026-06-18; Yahoo serves only ~60 calendar days of 5m history) |
| Sample | **60** complete regular sessions (09:30–16:00 ET), 78 five-minute bars each |
| Resolution model | break = first bar whose close exits the opening range; enter the *next* bar's open (1 lag); exit at session close |
| Regime note | QQQ buy-&-hold over the window = **+15.5 bps/day**, **62%** up-days — a short bull sample (named on every axis) |

> **Scope caveat (named on the axes).** The real sample is **60 days** — Yahoo's hard 5-minute
> history cap, not a choice. Sixty days cannot certify a positive intraday edge, but they are
> plenty to show the rule does **not** beat a random same-exposure entry (the spread is
> *negative*, not merely insignificant). The synthetic positive control proves the measurement
> engine *can* detect a planted ORB edge, so the real-tape null result is a finding, not a dead
> pipeline.

## Half 1 — the signal is NOT there (ORB vs same-exposure random entry, gross)

For each day the range breaks, we compare the ORB return to a random entry that holds the same
fraction of the session. `matched_dir` = same side, random time; `coin` = random side + time;
`drift` = always long (the day's drift). `t_vs0` is the t-stat of the ORB daily return against
zero; `t_paired` is the paired (ORB − random) t-stat; `perm_p` = P(random mean ≥ ORB mean).

| variant | null | trades | ORB bps/day | null bps/day | edge (ORB−null) | t vs 0 | t paired | hit | perm p |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| ORB 5m | matched_dir | 60 | −1.3 | +10.1 | **−11.3** | −0.10 | −1.32 | 48% | 0.992 |
| ORB 5m | coin | 60 | −1.3 | −0.1 | −1.2 | −0.10 | −0.80 | 48% | 0.552 |
| ORB 5m | drift | 60 | −1.3 | +8.1 | −9.4 | −0.10 | −0.86 | 48% | 0.976 |
| **ORB 15m** | **matched_dir** | **60** | **−2.5** | **+9.7** | **−12.2** | **−0.20** | **−1.78** | **45%** | **0.996** |
| ORB 15m | coin | 60 | −2.5 | −0.1 | −2.3 | −0.20 | −1.18 | 45% | 0.601 |
| ORB 15m | drift | 60 | −2.5 | +7.9 | −10.3 | −0.20 | −0.90 | 45% | 0.986 |

The ORB makes essentially **nothing** gross (−1 to −3 bps/day, t vs zero ≈ 0), and it **loses**
to a same-direction random entry by ~11–12 bps/day (perm p ≈ 0.99 — the random entry beats ORB
almost always). Breaking the morning range is, if anything, slightly *worse* than picking a
random minute and holding the same way. H₁ is rejected.

## Half 2 — costs only make it worse (one-way bps, ORB 15m vs matched-dir null)

| one-way cost | ORB net bps/day | edge over null | t vs 0 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps | −2.5 | −12.2 | −0.20 |
| 1 bp | −4.5 | −14.2 | −0.36 |
| 2 bps | −6.5 | −16.2 | −0.52 |
| 3 bps | −8.5 | −18.2 | −0.68 |
| 5 bps | −12.5 | −22.2 | −0.99 |

**Break-even one-way cost vs the null: −6.1 bps** — *negative*, meaning there is no cost level
at which ORB would beat the random entry; it is already behind gross. (Even ORB's raw return is
negative net of any spread.) H₂ is rejected for free.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

A deterministic AR(1)-per-bar day generator plants a *known* intraday trend-persistence (ORB
15m, matched-dir null, 800 days). The harness must recover a positive, significant
ORB-minus-random edge that grows with the persistence, and ~0 on a pure random walk:

| planted persistence | trades | ORB bps/day | null bps/day | edge | t paired | perm p | expectation |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| 0.00 (random walk) | 800 | +4.1 | +2.2 | +2.0 | +1.72 | 0.088 | edge ~0, not significant ✓ |
| 0.25 | 800 | +8.3 | +0.9 | +7.4 | +3.00 | 0.000 | edge > 0, significant ✓ |
| 0.40 | 800 | +11.8 | −0.8 | +12.6 | +3.64 | 0.000 | edge > 0, significant ✓ |

The measurement engine detects a real ORB edge **when one is planted** (monotone in the planted
persistence, t = 3.0–3.6) and finds **none on a random walk**. So the flat/negative real-tape
result is a property of the *market*, not a broken test.

## Cross-check — SPY tells the same story

SPY ORB 15m, matched-dir null: trades 59, ORB +1.5 bps/day, edge over null **−6.5 bps**,
t vs 0 +0.18, t paired −2.19. Same conclusion: no edge over a random same-exposure entry.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** On the real QQQ tape the ORB daily return is indistinguishable from zero
  (t vs 0 = −0.20) and **loses** to a same-exposure random entry by ~12 bps/day (paired
  t = −1.78, permutation p ≈ 0.996). SPY agrees. Breaking the opening range carries no
  directional information beyond the day's drift on this sample.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Break-even one-way cost vs the null is **negative** (−6.1 bps): no
  realistic spread/slippage makes ORB win, because it is already behind a random entry gross.
  Net of any cost the strategy is a small loser.
- **Beats a coin? — BUSTED.** The headline "ORB makes money" in a 60-day bull sample is the
  *drift*, not the breakout: a random same-exposure entry makes **more** (+9.7 bps vs −2.5).
  The signal that the rule claims to add is absent.

> **Caveat (named).** 60 trading days is a short, bull-only sample (Yahoo's 5m cap), so this
> cannot *disprove* the multi-year, leveraged, ATR-stopped ORB of Zarattini & Grewal (2023) on
> its own terms. What it does show, cleanly and reproducibly, is that the *bare* viral rule —
> break the range, hold to close — adds **nothing** over a random entry of equal exposure here,
> and that the engine would have caught a real edge if one were present.
